title: Photosynthesis explained simply
subtitle: Plants & energy
subject: sciences
description: Plants do something extraordinary: they cook sugar out of light, water, and air. And they hand us the oxygen as a gift.

hero.hook: A leaf is a solar kitchen: light, water, air, and out comes sugar.

blocks.text: Picture a tiny factory inside every leaf. It takes three ordinary ingredients: **sunlight**, the **water** drawn up by the roots, and the **CO₂** in the air. Out comes the **sugar** it needs to grow, plus the **oxygen** it releases.
This feat is called **photosynthesis**. Without it there would be no forests, no breathable oxygen, and almost no complex life on Earth.

sections.title: Where it happens in the leaf

blocks.text: Inside a plant cell, green compartments called **chloroplasts** hold the [[chlorophyll]]. This pigment mostly absorbs the blue and red parts of light. The green is bounced back, and that is why leaves look green to us.

The equation is simple: CO₂ plus water plus light gives sugar plus oxygen. The gas comes in through tiny pores, the [[stomata]]. The water climbs up from the roots. The sugar becomes wood, fruit, and roots, while the oxygen leaves for the air.
Chlorophyll “turns down” green. It prefers blue and red, which are better at exciting its electrons and starting the energy machine.
First comes the **light phase**. Light splits water molecules. The oxygen escapes. The energy is stored in two chemical “batteries,” **ATP** and **NADPH**.

Then comes the **building phase**, the [[Calvin cycle]], named after the chemist **Melvin Calvin**. Using the energy in those batteries, the plant assembles the carbon from CO₂ into glucose. This step needs no direct sunlight, but it depends entirely on what the light produced earlier.
To follow the path of carbon through a leaf, Calvin used radioactive isotopes that came out of atomic bomb research. Nobel Prize in **1961**.

About **2.4 billion years ago**, photosynthetic bacteria called **cyanobacteria** began releasing oxygen in huge amounts. This was the **Great Oxidation Event**. For many organisms of the time, it was a poison.
Oxygen then made the ozone layer possible, along with far more efficient breathing. The air we breathe is, broadly speaking, the “waste” from billions of years of photosynthesis.
About **half** of Earth's oxygen comes from ocean phytoplankton, not only from forests.

sections.title: A modest yield, a huge role

blocks.text: A leaf turns only **1 to 3%** of the solar energy it receives into biomass. On the scale of the whole planet, that is still enough to feed the food chains and to soak up enormous amounts of CO₂.

That is why forests, oceans, and even artificial photosynthesis matter so much for the climate. One sea slug, *Elysia chlorotica*, goes as far as “stealing” chloroplasts from algae so it can live partly on solar power.
Photosynthesis turns light, water, and CO₂ into sugar, and puts oxygen back into the air. It is the solar kitchen at the base of almost all life.
